extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and literary critics (particularly writers of heroic/epic poetry and heroic drama)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for composing heroic poems and heroic plays: how to handle unity, grandeur, supernatural machinery, spectacle, characterisation, and plausibility in epic/heroic verse and staged heroic drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and greatness of action
rubrics_metrics.description: An heroic poem should be 'one entire and great action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The laws of an heroic poem do not dispense with the laws of other poetry but raise them to a greater height; the work should present a single, elevated action rather than a scattered or trivial series of incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery and design must match majesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Images and overall design must be proportioned to the greatness and majesty of an heroic poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'scanting of his images and design' — the poet must supply grand, ample imagery and structure appropriate to the heroic scale. Insufficient imagery/design is a fault when the subject demands grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not merely historical narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic poetry is not to be reduced to historicizing narration ('Non enim res gestæ versibus comprehendendæ sunt...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat epic as sober history; rather than compressing events like a historian, use poetical devices, divine machinery, and 'furentis animi vaticinatio' (prophetic/exalted inspiration) to convey the spirit and vision of the poem. Avoid overcrowding verse with dry historical detail or epigrammatic points (criticisms made of Lucan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of gods, spirits, and supernatural machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: The inclusion of gods, spirits, visions, and magical or visionary scenes is a legitimate and often necessary part of heroic poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancients and great moderns (Homer, Virgil, Tasso, Spencer) used supernatural elements to produce some of their finest beauties (e.g., Polydorus' ghost, Tasso's Enchanted Wood, Spencer's Bower of Bliss). Such elements give scope for imagination and can explicate doubtful metaphysical problems more poetically than philosophical prose. Their use need not be literally probable to be justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permission for visionary and improbable elements
rubrics_metrics.description: An heroic poet is not tied to bare representation of what is true or strictly probable; he may let himself loose to visionary objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What 'may be in nature' is sufficient foundation for poetry; poets may describe things beyond sense to expand imaginative scope. Improbability is not an automatic fault provided the elements are poetically defensible and help the poem's grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid converting epic into a 'play in narration'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not simply model an heroic poem on the drama by dividing it into acts/cantos to imitate stage scenes ('rather a play in narration').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden rejects the idea of dressing epic in too familiar or stage-like a form — the epic should maintain its own elevated mode rather than be trimmed down to the 'common actions and passions' of drama. Imitating stage-acts too literally reduces the poem's scope and dignity (critique of proposals to divide into five books representing acts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical spectacle and stage devices when dramatizing
rubrics_metrics.description: In heroic plays, use spectacle (drums, trumpets, representations of battles) to raise the audience's imagination and persuade them the action is really performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The drama's advantage is visible representation: 'Segnius irritant animum demissa per aures, quam quæ sunt oculis subjecta fidelibus.' Stage noises and presentations (as used by Shakespeare and others) are legitimate means to produce the effects required of an heroic play; the poet should help the audience's fancy rather than rely on it alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet should seek dominion over spectators' minds
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer ought to help and aim for 'absolute dominion over the minds of the spectators.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must deliberately manipulate stagecraft and rhetoric to govern audience imagination; do not expect fancy alone to supply needed effects. Using proven devices (even if used by mountebanks) is justified if they aid the play's persuasive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroic characters must be grand yet human
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroes should be men of great spirit who retain human passions and frailties rather than being austerely perfect moral exemplars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model heroes (Achilles, Rinaldo) exhibit honour and greatness but also anger, impatience, and other human traits; the poet should show what great-spirited men would do when provoked, not what strict moral virtue would demand. This produces more convincing, interesting characters than over-sanitized exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject over-refined moral scruples in character (anti-French standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid subjecting characters to the French standard where love and honour are weighed by scruples and measured drams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden criticises the French tendency to overmeasure honour and romantic feeling; such excessive scrupulosity makes heroes less natural and diminishes the poetry. Do not allow restraint by artificial codes to curtail spirited, plausible heroic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility vs. impossibility — justify daring actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Admit daring or improbable deeds if they are not impossible and can be grounded in character, circumstance, or historical precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticisms that a hero 'performs impossibilities' can be answered by showing precedent (e.g., Caesar calming mutinies) or by contextualizing the hero's reputation and circumstances. Improbable does not equal impossible; explain how extraordinary feats are plausible within the narrative and character framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: On imitation and originality when writing after greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers who follow great predecessors face the curse to 'write better, or you else write worse' — mere equality seems theft or borrowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing in a genre with towering predecessors (Shakespeare, Homer, Virgil), aim to bring something new or higher; slavish imitation risks being judged inferior. Praise is more valuable when true and not merely comparative flattery.
